# Claude Code Field Notes: Running AI Coding Agents in Production

> Six lessons from running 20+ live software surfaces with Claude Code and AI coding agents: verification, silent config failures, deploy safety and worktrees.

Source: https://claude.suedeai.ai/
Author: Jason Colapietro (Johnny Suede), founder and CEO of Suede AI (https://suedeai.ai/founder)
Published: 2026-07-27

Abridged from The Complete Claude Code Compendium. Each lesson below is the full text of its page.

## Lesson 1: A clean build is a compile check, not proof

Source: https://claude.suedeai.ai/clean-build-is-not-proof/

> A wallet-connect refactor passed build, type-check, and lint, then broke a live button. Verify the artifact you shipped by doing the thing a user does.

A wallet-connect refactor passed build, type-check, and lint. It merged and deployed under standing autonomy. Then it broke a live button on six marketing pages with a client-side exception the instant anyone clicked it.

Nothing in the pipeline was wrong. The pipeline answers "does this compile and typecheck," and the question that mattered was "does the button still work." Those are different questions and only one of them was being asked.

The rule that came out of it: **verify the artifact you shipped, by doing the thing a user does.** For an interactive change that means clicking it on the live domain, in a clean browser context, after the deploy lands. It cost ten minutes to catch and revert. It would have cost nothing to prevent.

Two corollaries worth adopting:

- **Verify the committed state, not your working tree.** A passing test against uncommitted local files proves nothing about what you pushed.

- **Verify against the live URL, not the build log.** A green deploy and a working page are different claims.

## Lesson 2: An empty environment variable is worse than a missing one

Source: https://claude.suedeai.ai/empty-environment-variables/

> Environment variables that resolve as empty strings pass as valid input and trigger silent fallbacks. Assert configuration at startup and fail loudly.

A production outage traced back to environment variables resolving as empty strings rather than being absent. The code read them, found empty values, and took a silent fallback path: from a durable Postgres store to an ephemeral local one, inside a serverless function, with no error raised anywhere.

A missing variable crashes at boot and you find out in thirty seconds. An empty one is valid input. The system keeps running and quietly does the wrong thing.

**Assert your configuration at startup, and make the assertion fail loudly.** Then verify the datastore's identity from production itself rather than from your intent. If your config says Postgres, ask production what it is actually writing to.

## Lesson 3: Money-path defaults must fail closed

Source: https://claude.suedeai.ai/money-path-defaults-fail-closed/

> A settlement toggle shipped opt-in, and every paid endpoint became free to call while billing reported itself live. Choose the default that fails safe.

A settlement toggle shipped opt-in, defaulting to false. Production was missing the column entirely, so every priced endpoint mapped to dry-run, and dry-run skipped the payment challenge. The result: every paid endpoint was free to call, while the billing system reported itself live.

The fix inverted the default. Missing or null now means charge; only an explicit toggle disables it.

The generalization applies past payments to any control whose failure is expensive: **when a default must be wrong in one direction, choose the direction that fails safe.** For revenue, absence should mean charge. For access, absence should mean deny.

## Lesson 4: Deploy conventions are attack surface

Source: https://claude.suedeai.ai/deploy-conventions-are-attack-surface/

> On route-mapped platforms every file is a public URL, so a colocated test file turns into an unauthenticated endpoint. Audit the deployed site, not the repo.

On some platforms, every file in a specific directory becomes a public HTTP route. Filename maps to URL, with no other gate. That convention is convenient until a colocated test file lands there.

A file named something.test.js in that directory is not a test. It is an unauthenticated endpoint that executes a test suite inside a production function when anyone requests it, boots whatever servers the test defines, and holds the invocation open toward the platform's timeout ceiling. Anyone who finds it can loop it.

The audit is one line per candidate file, and it checks production rather than your file tree:

```
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' https://<domain>/api/<basename>
```

Anything that is not a real endpoint should answer 404. **Treat every file under a route-mapped directory as a public URL, and confirm it against the deployed site rather than the repository.** Framework conventions differ, so learn which of yours maps filenames to routes.

## Lesson 5: A registry reports what it was told; a process table reports what is

Source: https://claude.suedeai.ai/registry-vs-process-table/

> A session registry reported live agent workspaces as not running. Ask the operating system with lsof, and re-check immediately before deleting anything.

During a cleanup of finished agent workspaces, the session registry reported several as not running. They had live processes inside them with child processes actively writing files. Acting on the registry would have deleted a running agent's workspace mid-edit.

The check that works asks the operating system, not the bookkeeping:

```
lsof -d cwd 2>/dev/null | grep "<path>"
```

Two things make this worse than it sounds. **Workspaces go live while you audit them**, so a directory that was idle ten minutes ago is not evidence about now; re-check immediately before deleting. And **squash-merged branches look unmerged**: commit ancestry shows work ahead of main even when the content already landed, because main moved on. Use git cherry or match commit subjects rather than trusting ancestry, or you will keep dead workspaces and, worse, convince yourself that merged work was lost.

## Lesson 6: When documentation is silent, measure

Source: https://claude.suedeai.ai/when-documentation-is-silent-measure/

> Capture a payload instead of guessing at its shape. A hook that logs its input answers in a minute, and the installed binary is the source of truth.

Documentation for agent tooling ages faster than it is written. Rather than guessing at a payload shape, capture one. A hook that dumps its input to disk answers the question in a minute, for the exact version you are running:

```
#!/bin/bash
payload=$(cat)
printf '%s\n' "$payload" >> /tmp/probe/events.jsonl
exit 0
```

Point every event you care about at that script, run one throwaway session, and read the log. Doing this surfaced a documented event whose handler-type table omitted it, even though a handler on that event demonstrably fires. **The installed binary is the source of truth. Documentation is a secondary source, and version-gated features make it a moving one.**

## Note: Nine Claude Academy badges, one West Palm Beach agency: what the courses cover and what production added

Source: https://claude.suedeai.ai/notes/claude-academy-badges-west-palm-beach-agency/
Published: 2026-11-14

> Jason Colapietro holds nine Claude Academy badges. What the courses teach, what running Suede AI's West Palm Beach agency on Claude Code added, and what to ask.

Jason Colapietro holds nine Claude Academy badges, and none of them would have caught the wallet-connect button that broke on six live pages. That is not a knock on the courses. It is the most useful thing to know about any credential before you hire an agency on the strength of one, Suede AI included.

This note covers what the nine badges are, what the courses actually teach, and what running a West Palm Beach agency on Claude Code added on top.

### What the nine badges are

The badges are Anthropic course credentials earned through Claude Academy. Three carry most of the weight for agency work: **Claude Code 101**, **Building with the Claude API**, and **Model Context Protocol: Advanced topics**. They sit inside a larger record of 21 earned individual course credentials across eight providers, which also includes five Semrush Academy certificates (Local SEO Essentials and AI Search Operating System among them), the HubSpot AEO Fundamentals certification, two Google Skills badges, a Databricks Generative AI Fundamentals accreditation and an IBM SkillsBuild credential. On top of those sit 17 Microsoft Learn training achievements, including the "Develop AI agents on Azure" learning-path trophy.

Every one is linked from the [Suede AI training-credential gallery](https://seo.suedeai.ai/evidence#training-credentials), where Jason Colapietro keeps the issuer link for each badge. Suede publishes the gallery because a claim without a receipt is just copy. The same evidence page records that Suede AI has been a member of [Claude for Startups, Anthropic's startup program](https://seo.suedeai.ai/evidence#claude-for-startups), since October 8, 2026. That is program membership, and we describe it that way. Suede AI ranks among [Clutch](https://clutch.co/profile/suede-ai-seo)'s [Top 30 AI Consultants in Florida](https://clutch.co/consulting/ai/florida) and [Top 50 AI Consultants nationwide](https://clutch.co/us/consulting/ai) (November 2026).

### What the courses actually teach

Claude Code 101 teaches the working loop: give the agent a scoped task, let it read the repository, review what it proposes, and keep a project memory file so the next session starts with the house rules. Building with the Claude API covers the layer underneath: messages, tool definitions, streaming, and the cost and latency tradeoffs between model tiers. The MCP course covers how an agent reaches outside the repository through Model Context Protocol servers. For an agency, that is where the real exposure sits, because an MCP server is a credentialed door into a client's systems.

All three do one thing well. They teach how the tool is supposed to behave. A credential confirms that someone worked through the material and passed the checks. It says nothing about what happens when four sessions are open against twenty production surfaces late on a Thursday.

### What production added

Jason Colapietro runs the Suede AI production estate himself, with coding agents doing most of the typing. The six [Claude Code Field Notes lessons](https://claude.suedeai.ai/) came out of that estate, and each one fills a gap the coursework leaves open.

- **Green is not working.** Courses teach you to run the tests. Production taught that a passing build and a working button are separate claims, so every interactive change gets clicked on the live domain after deploy. See [a clean build is a compile check, not proof](https://claude.suedeai.ai/clean-build-is-not-proof/).

- **Configuration fails quietly.** No module covers an environment variable that resolves to an empty string and reroutes writes to an ephemeral store. Production did. See [an empty environment variable is worse than a missing one](https://claude.suedeai.ai/empty-environment-variables/).

- **Bookkeeping drifts.** The MCP course explains how servers register. It does not warn that a session registry can report a workspace idle while a live agent writes inside it. See [registry versus process table](https://claude.suedeai.ai/registry-vs-process-table/).

- **Docs trail the binary.** Course material is a snapshot of one version. When a hook payload was undocumented, the answer came from logging the payload. See [when documentation is silent, measure](https://claude.suedeai.ai/when-documentation-is-silent-measure/).

The shape repeats, and it is why Suede treats a badge as a starting point. The course taught the intended behavior, and production showed where the reported state and the real state split apart.

### How the agency uses both

Suede AI's [West Palm Beach SEO, GEO and web practice](https://suedeai.agency/) maintains websites for businesses across Palm Beach County, from Jupiter and Juno Beach down to Boca Raton, and coding agents touch every one of those repositories. The training shows up in three places.

**Scoping.** The Claude Code 101 habit of narrow tasks and a memory file is how each client repository starts. The file lists the build commands, the pages that carry revenue, and the things an agent may never change, such as DNS, payment settings or analytics tags.

**Tool boundaries.** The MCP material is why client connections are read-only by default. An agent can read a Search Console export or an analytics report. It cannot publish, delete or touch billing without a human step.

**Proof.** Production is why each change ships with evidence: the command that ran, the URL that was checked, the before and after. It is the same standard behind Suede's [technical SEO service](https://suedeai.agency/services/technical-seo) and its [AI visibility work](https://suedeai.agency/services/ai-visibility).

### What to ask any agency that uses coding agents

If you run a business in West Palm Beach and are weighing an agency that builds with AI agents, ask two questions. First, ask for the credentials, with links you can open. Second, ask what broke in production last quarter and what rule came out of it. The first answer tells you someone studied. The second tells you someone has been on call.

Jason has written his answer to the second question at book length. He is the author of five books on Amazon, including [The Claude Code Bible](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HHTMJWB4) and [Codex in Production](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HHTF3LG1). He also has [54 pull requests merged across 46 open-source repositories he does not maintain](https://github.com/search?q=is%3Apr+author%3AJasonColapietro+is%3Amerged+-user%3AJasonColapietro+-user%3ASuede-AI&type=pullrequests), including Jest, Adobe React Spectrum, Backstage and the Polkadot SDK. A merged pull request in someone else's project is the closest thing software has to a reference check: a maintainer who owed Jason Colapietro nothing had to accept the change.

Suede AI, formerly Suede Labs, was founded in 2024 as an agentic platform company. Search visibility is one service line, and these notes are where the engineering habits behind it get written down.

### Next step

If agents already maintain your site, or you want them to, start with the [Suede AI site assessment](https://suedeai.agency/assessment). It reviews your site the way these notes describe: against the live URL, with receipts. For background on Jason Colapietro, see the [founder page](https://suedeai.ai/founder).

## Note: From The Claude Code Bible to client work: a field guide for South Florida dev teams adopting coding agents

Source: https://claude.suedeai.ai/notes/claude-code-bible-south-florida-dev-teams/
Published: 2026-11-14

> A four-week plan for Palm Beach County dev teams moving from The Claude Code Bible to client work with coding agents: memory files, gates, worktrees, limits.

Most dev teams in Palm Beach County do not need a strategy deck to start with coding agents. They need a first month that does not end with an agent pushing an untested change to a client's production site on a Friday afternoon.

This is the four-week version of what Jason Colapietro wrote at length in [The Claude Code Bible](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HHTMJWB4), adapted for the teams Suede AI talks to most: small agencies and in-house developers in West Palm Beach, Jupiter, Palm Beach Gardens and Boca Raton, usually a handful of engineers, usually maintaining client sites rather than one product.

### Week one: one repository, one memory file

Pick a repository where a mistake is cheap. A marketing site with a preview deploy is ideal. Do not start on the codebase that takes payments.

Before the first prompt, write the project memory file (CLAUDE.md, or AGENTS.md with a one-line CLAUDE.md that imports it). Keep it short and specific:

- The exact commands that must pass before a commit: type-check, lint, test, build.

- The directories an agent may not touch, such as infrastructure, secrets and payment configuration.

- House rules for commits and branches, including whether to push at all.

Every session reads that file first. It is the cheapest control you will ever add, and the one teams skip most. Jason Colapietro keeps one in every Suede AI repository, this site included.

### Week two: gates before the merge

The second week is about the difference between "the agent said it is done" and "it is done." Agents run the gates; people read the diffs. Run the gates against the committed state, not a working tree full of uncommitted edits:

```
git stash -u && npm run typecheck && npm run lint && npm test && npm run build; git stash pop
```

Then add the step most teams miss: check the deployed page. A green pipeline proves the code compiles. It does not prove the contact form still submits. Field Notes lesson 1, [a clean build is a compile check, not proof](https://claude.suedeai.ai/clean-build-is-not-proof/), is the incident that made this rule permanent at Suede.

### Week three: parallel sessions without collisions

Once one agent is reliable, someone will open three. Give each its own git worktree and its own branch, so two sessions never edit the same checkout. When you clean up, ask the operating system which workspaces are live rather than trusting a list:

```
lsof -d cwd 2>/dev/null | grep "<worktree path>"
```

Two traps from [lesson 5](https://claude.suedeai.ai/registry-vs-process-table/) are worth posting on the wall. A workspace that was idle ten minutes ago may be busy now, so re-check right before deleting. And squash-merged branches look unmerged to commit ancestry, so use git cherry before you decide work was lost.

### Week four: client repositories

Client work adds two things the tutorials rarely cover: other people's credentials and other people's revenue.

**Credentials.** Keep secrets out of prompts and out of the memory file. Give agents read-only MCP access to analytics and search data by default, and keep publishing, DNS and billing behind a human. Assert configuration at startup so an empty variable fails loudly, as in [lesson 2](https://claude.suedeai.ai/empty-environment-variables/).

**Revenue.** Any toggle that touches checkout or billing should fail closed: if the setting is missing, charge, and if access is unclear, deny. [Lesson 3](https://claude.suedeai.ai/money-path-defaults-fail-closed/) is the story of what happens otherwise. If the client's host maps files in a directory to public routes, audit the deployed site for stray files, as in [lesson 4](https://claude.suedeai.ai/deploy-conventions-are-attack-surface/).

### What the book adds and what this guide leaves out

The Claude Code Bible is the long version, written for one operator learning the tool end to end. This guide compresses it into a team rollout and drops everything that does not change week-one behavior. Teams running Codex alongside Claude Code will want [Codex in Production](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HHTF3LG1), which applies the same verification habits to the other tool.

Both books come out of daily operating experience. Jason Colapietro ships agent-assisted work across the Suede AI estate, has shipped [nine iOS apps under his own Apple developer account](https://apps.apple.com/us/developer/jason-colapietro/id1895958699), and has [54 pull requests merged across 46 open-source repositories he does not maintain](https://github.com/search?q=is%3Apr+author%3AJasonColapietro+is%3Amerged+-user%3AJasonColapietro+-user%3ASuede-AI&type=pullrequests), including Jest and Backstage. The plan above is the subset of that practice Jason thinks a small team can adopt in a month. Suede AI ranks among [Clutch](https://clutch.co/profile/suede-ai-seo)'s [Top 30 AI Consultants in Florida](https://clutch.co/consulting/ai/florida) and [Top 50 AI Consultants nationwide](https://clutch.co/us/consulting/ai) (November 2026).

### Where teams usually stall

The common failure is not a bad prompt. It is skipping week two because week one felt fast. Agents make the first draft cheap, which moves the cost to review, and a team that does not plan for review time ends up merging diffs nobody read. Budget review time on purpose. Jason Colapietro's working rule is that the hour an agent saves on writing should be partly spent on checking, and he writes that rule into each Suede AI project plan.

The second stall is tooling sprawl: five MCP servers wired up in week one, none of them scoped. Add one connection at a time, read-only first, and write down what each one can reach. For MCP documentation patterns written for agencies, the [Suede developer docs notes](https://docs.suedeai.ai/notes) go deeper. To score an agent's behavior before you trust it with client work, the [Agentix grader notes](https://agentix.suedeai.ai/notes) describe how Suede grades agents.

### Next step

If your South Florida team wants a second set of eyes on its first month, book the [Suede AI assessment](https://suedeai.agency/assessment) through the agency site. You will get a review of your repository setup and your live site, with every finding tied to a command or a URL. More on Jason Colapietro is on the [founder page](https://suedeai.ai/founder).

## Note: Agent-written code still needs proof: how Suede AI reviews AI changes before they ship

Source: https://claude.suedeai.ai/notes/reviewing-agent-written-code/
Published: 2026-11-14

> How Suede AI reviews agent-written code before it ships: diff review against callers, gates on the committed state, live-URL checks and a receipt per change.

An agent can write a plausible diff in minutes. Reviewing it properly takes longer than that, and the gap between those two numbers is where most agent-written bugs get through. At Suede AI the answer is not to slow the agent down. It is to make the review mechanical enough that it actually happens every time.

This note is the review process Jason Colapietro runs on agent-written changes across the Suede AI estate and on client sites maintained from West Palm Beach. It has three layers and ends with a receipt.

### Layer one: read the diff against its callers

Agents are good at making the changed lines look right. They are weaker at the code that calls those lines. So the first read starts outside the diff:

- Who calls the changed function, and does every caller still get what it expects?

- Did a default change? Defaults are where an "optional" refactor quietly alters behavior for every existing user.

- Did a file land in a directory the platform serves as public routes?

- Is there a deleted check, a widened permission or a new network call the task did not ask for?

Each finding gets a severity from P0 to P3 and a file and line. A P0 blocks the merge. A P3 goes in a follow-up. The open-source [Suede AI code review skill](https://skills.suedeai.ai/skills/suede-code.html) encodes the same pass, so an agent can run it on another agent's work before a person reads it.

### Layer two: gates on the committed state

Jason Colapietro calls the gates the boring part, and they are the part most often run wrong. They must run against what was committed, not against a working tree that still holds uncommitted fixes. A fresh clone of the branch is the cleanest way:

```
git clone --branch "$BRANCH" --depth 1 "$REPO" /tmp/review && cd /tmp/review
npm ci && npm run typecheck && npm run lint && npm test && npm run build
```

If the repository has a guard test for its own rules, such as banned copy, schema ids or sitemap entries, it runs here too. Suede never weakens a guard to get a green run. If a guard blocks a change, the change is wrong or the guard needs a reviewed update in its own commit.

### Layer three: proof on the live URL

After the deploy lands, check the thing a user touches. For a content change, that is the page itself, its canonical URL and its structured data. For an interactive change, it is a click in a clean browser profile. For a route change, it is the status codes:

```
for path in / /notes/ /api/healthz /api/handler.test; do
  printf '%s %s\n' "$(curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://example.com$path")" "$path"
done
```

Pages should answer 200 and anything that is not a real endpoint should answer 404. [Lesson 4](https://claude.suedeai.ai/deploy-conventions-are-attack-surface/) covers why the last line in that loop matters. [Lesson 1](https://claude.suedeai.ai/clean-build-is-not-proof/) covers why none of this can be replaced by a build log.

### What goes in the receipt

Every reviewed change leaves a short record. It is plain text, and it fits in a commit message or a pull request description:

- The commit SHA that was reviewed and deployed.

- Each command that ran, with its exit code.

- Each URL that was checked, with its status and what was looked at.

- What was not checked, stated plainly.

The last line is the one that builds trust. A receipt that claims everything was verified is less believable than one that says the checkout flow was not exercised because it needs a real card.

### Why Suede publishes receipts in public

The same habit runs through how Suede AI talks about itself. Every public claim has a proof link on the [Suede AI evidence page](https://seo.suedeai.ai/evidence). When we say that on October 31, 2026, Suede AI SEO ranked #1 among Palm Beach County-based companies listed in [The Manifest's Florida AI Deployment directory](https://themanifest.com/artificial-intelligence/consulting/deployment/companies/florida) and in the top 25 statewide, the directory link and the [recognition page](https://suedeai.agency/company/recognition) sit next to it. Suede AI ranks among [Clutch](https://clutch.co/profile/suede-ai-seo)'s [Top 30 AI Consultants in Florida](https://clutch.co/consulting/ai/florida) and [Top 50 AI Consultants nationwide](https://clutch.co/us/consulting/ai) (November 2026). When we cite Jason Colapietro's [54 merged pull requests across 46 open-source repositories he does not maintain](https://github.com/search?q=is%3Apr+author%3AJasonColapietro+is%3Amerged+-user%3AJasonColapietro+-user%3ASuede-AI&type=pullrequests), the search that produces the number is the link.

Open-source review is also where this process was tested hardest. Maintainers of projects like Jest, Adobe React Spectrum and the Polkadot SDK do not accept a change because an agent was confident. They accept it because the change is small, tested and explained, which is the standard Suede applies to its own work. Suede AI, formerly Suede Labs, holds internal changes to the same bar it meets in other people's repositories.

### The cost, stated plainly

This process is slower than merging on a green check. Every change gains a review pass and a live check, and that is real time on the calendar. We accept the cost because the alternative was measured too: the broken wallet button from lesson 1 took ten minutes to catch and revert after it reached users, plus the time it was live. Review time is predictable. Incident time is not.

Jason is direct about the limits. It does not catch everything. Live checks sample the paths that matter most; they do not exercise every branch. That is why the receipt names what was skipped, and why Jason Colapietro treats a missing line in a receipt as a finding in its own right.

### Next step

If agents write code for your website, ask your developer for one receipt from last week. If they cannot produce one, the [Suede AI assessment](https://suedeai.agency/assessment) is a good place to start. It applies this review to your live site and hands back findings you can verify yourself. For the person behind the process, see Jason Colapietro's [founder page](https://suedeai.ai/founder), and for an AI readiness check of your pages, the [Suede Scan notes](https://optimize.suedeai.ai/notes).

## The pattern underneath

Every lesson here is the same shape. A system reported success while doing something else: a green build, an empty variable, a billing toggle, a file tree, a session registry, a documentation page. In each case the fix was to ask the thing itself instead of asking a record of it.

That gets more expensive to ignore as you add agents. One person reviewing one change can hold the gap between reported and actual in their head. Six concurrent agents shipping against twenty surfaces cannot, so the verification has to be mechanical and it has to run against production.
